snapshot.exam_hook: ⚡ TNPSC Economy Hook: Tendulkar: Poverty. Lorenz: Inequality. Gini: 0 to 1. Disguised: Agri. Nurkse: Vicious Circle.

quick_notes.title: Poverty Line Concepts
quick_notes.detail: Absolute Poverty (Minimum physical requirements). Relative Poverty (Inequality compared to others). HCR (Head Count Ratio).
quick_notes.explanation: Absolute poverty means a person does not have enough money to meet the minimum physical needs for survival, like food, water, and shelter. Relative poverty compares a person's income or resources to other people in the same society, so even if they have enough to survive, they may still be considered poor if they have much less than others. The Head Count Ratio, or HCR, is a measurement that shows the percentage of people in a population who live below the poverty line.

quick_notes.title: Committees on Poverty
quick_notes.detail: 1. Lakdawala (1993). 2. Tendulkar (2009 - shifted to per capita exp). 3. Rangarajan (2014).
quick_notes.explanation: The Indian government has set up committees over the years to decide how to measure poverty, which means figuring out who does not have enough money for basic needs. The first committee, led by Lakdawala in 1993, calculated a poverty line based on how much people spent on food to get a minimum number of calories. In 2009, the Tendulkar committee changed the method to use per capita expenditure, which is the average amount of money each person spends on all goods and services, not just food. The most recent committee, led by Rangarajan in 2014, created a new poverty line that included spending on food, education, health, and other essentials. Each committee's poverty line is a specific amount of money per person per month that separates the poor from the non-poor.

quick_notes.title: Types of Unemployment
quick_notes.detail: Structural (Mismatch of skills), Frictional (Temporary), Cyclical (Recession), Disguised (Agriculture).
quick_notes.explanation: Unemployment means people who are able and willing to work but cannot find a job. Structural unemployment happens when workers do not have the skills that employers need, so their skills do not match the available jobs. Frictional unemployment is the short, temporary period when someone is between jobs, like after quitting or graduating. Cyclical unemployment occurs during a recession, which is a period when the economy slows down and companies produce less, so they hire fewer workers. Disguised unemployment is common in agriculture, where more people are working on a farm than are actually needed, so even if some stop working, the total output does not change.

quick_notes.title: Lorenz Curve & Gini Coefficient
quick_notes.detail: Measure of Income Inequality. 0 : Perfect equality, 1 : Perfect inequality.
quick_notes.explanation: The Lorenz Curve is a graph that shows how income or wealth is distributed across a population. It plots the cumulative share of total income received against the cumulative share of people, starting from the poorest. The Gini Coefficient is a single number calculated from the Lorenz Curve that measures the level of income inequality.

quick_notes.title: Vicious Circle of Poverty
quick_notes.detail: Concept by Ragnar Nurkse: "A country is poor because it is poor" (Low income -> Low savings -> Low investment).
quick_notes.explanation: The Vicious Circle of Poverty is a theory by economist Ragnar Nurkse that explains why poor countries stay poor. The idea is a cycle: a country has very low income, meaning people earn very little money. Because income is low, people cannot save much money, so savings are low. With low savings, the country has little money to invest in things like factories, roads, or machines that could increase production. Without investment, the country cannot produce more goods or create more jobs, so incomes stay low. This completes the circle, which is why Nurkse said that a country is poor simply because it is poor.
